Preservation

The personal web was built across thousands of services, tools, communities, and image hosts. This page is about what happened as that infrastructure changed or disappeared, and the people and projects that kept parts of it alive.

For the focused history of glitter graphics and the culture around them, see History.

Contents

  1. Why Preservation Matters
  2. Timeline

Why Preservation Matters

In the 1990s, being online often meant making a place of your own, partly because there wasn't much else on the internet yet. If you wanted a homepage, a profile, a collection of things you liked, or some kind of social space, you had to build it yourself. People made pages, decorated them, made graphics, linked to friends, joined webrings and communities, and invented their own ways of interacting. A lot of what websites now handle automatically had to be put together by hand.

For a while in the 2000s, all these different versions of the web existed at once: personal websites, blogs, instant messengers, forums, virtual worlds, art communities, customizable profiles, image hosts, bookmarking sites, and social networks. There wasn't one standard way a social website was supposed to work yet.

That started to change as more of the web moved onto bigger platforms. The social networks of the 2000s still left room for customization, but more of the structure came pre-built. You didn't need to make a page of friends when the site could generate a friends list for you, or maintain a links page when it could organize your connections. More and more of the work shifted from building the structure yourself to deciding what to put inside a structure someone else had already made. Eventually much of the social web settled into the same basic structure: profiles, feeds, likes, comments, and follows.

People kept making things online, but the places where they could shape how they appeared became much more limited. Personal websites had often relied on image hosts too, especially when storage or bandwidth was limited, but those images could still be arranged into a page you designed yourself. On larger platforms, customization increasingly meant choosing a profile picture, adding a header or background, and deciding what to post. The surrounding layout belonged to the platform and looked essentially the same for everyone. The parts you could customize became smaller islands inside a design you no longer controlled.

The web people built by hand was easy to break. A personal site might be hosted in one place, pull its images from another, depend on Flash or some other plugin, embed a chatbox from another service, use an off-site hit counter, and belong to a community hosted somewhere else entirely. A lot of what looked like one website was actually assembled from pieces provided by several different services. If one piece disappeared, the page might still load, but part of what it was meant to show or do was gone. Enough missing pieces could strip away its design, functionality, and even some of its information while leaving the basic HTML behind. Image hosting makes this especially obvious: huge parts of the old web survive as HTML, while the externally hosted graphics that actually made up those pages are gone.

Many of those dependencies were controlled by companies the people using them had no say over. Services got bought, shut down, or changed their business model, sometimes with consequences far beyond the service itself. Polyvore ran for more than a decade before its site disappeared the same day SSENSE announced it had acquired Polyvore's assets. Yahoo stripped the web-accessible content out of Yahoo Groups before shutting the service down completely. Photobucket put third-party image hosting behind a paid plan and instantly broke images across forums, blogs, shops, and websites it didn't even own.

The old infrastructure disappeared unevenly. A lot of services from the personal-homepage era shut down in the late 2000s and early 2010s, while others hung around much longer. AOL dial-up lasted until 2025. In 2026, Lycos announced the shutdown of Angelfire and Tripod, and both eventually went dark. Some of these services outlived the version of the web they came from by decades.

What disappeared with them was much of the easy entry point. Free hosts had given people somewhere to experiment without first paying for anything or understanding domains, hosting plans, servers, or how any of that infrastructure worked. You could decide you wanted a website and start making one. Once more of those services disappeared, building a site was still completely possible, but the first step became a little harder, especially for someone who wasn't yet sure they wanted to spend money on a hobby.

The instability of the web was obvious enough that even ordinary tools were built around it. Google's cached results could provide a copy when the original page or server was unavailable. When Google removed the feature in 2024, it said it had been created for a time when pages were much less reliable and that the web had since improved. That change also reflects a more centralized web, where much of what people encounter now lives on a smaller number of large, professionally maintained platforms rather than being scattered across independent hosts and services.

People have been trying to keep the web from disappearing for almost as long as it has existed. The Internet Archive was founded in 1996, and the Wayback Machine went public in 2001. Other projects approached the same problem in their own ways. Neocities gave people an easy platform to build personal websites again, while the Internet Archive's GifCities made graphics recovered from GeoCities searchable. The Palace survived in a more literal sense: Communities.com stopped officially supporting it and later went bankrupt, but users kept running their own Palace communities without them.

That gets harder when so much material is concentrated inside a few large platforms and publishers, because they can decide whether anyone is allowed to archive it. In 2025, Reddit restricted the Internet Archive from crawling most posts, comments, and profiles, saying AI companies had been scraping Reddit content through the Wayback Machine and raising concerns about deleted material remaining available there. Major news publishers have begun restricting the Archive too, stating that the concern has largely been that archived copies provide another route for AI companies to access copyrighted journalism, but those archives also preserve articles before they are edited, removed, redesigned, or placed behind different access restrictions. Without them, it becomes much harder to see what a page said at a particular point in time. A web concentrated in fewer places may be more technically reliable, but it also gives a relatively small number of companies much more control over what survives as part of its historical record.

Websites, graphics, profiles, forum posts, and entire communities are now old enough to count as historical artifacts, and a lot of the originals are already gone. Much of what's left survives only because somebody saved a file, archived a page, mirrored a site, or kept something running after the company behind it stopped caring.

Timeline

A chronology of the platforms, programs, and websites that shaped the personal web: when they launched, when they changed hands, and when (or if) they went dark.

Last updated 14 September 2026
  • 1969ARPANET sends its first message, the starting point for what would evolve into the modern internet.
  • 1980Usenet is established, a worldwide distributed discussion system built on the Unix-to-Unix Copy (UUCP) dial-up network architecture. Tom Truscott and Jim Ellis had conceived the idea the year before, in 1979.
  • 1 May 1985Quantum Computer Services launches the Q-Link online service for Commodore 64 users; it's renamed America Online (AOL) in 1989.
  • 15 Jun 1987The GIF format is released by a team at CompuServe led by Steve Wilhite.
  • 19 Feb 1990Adobe Photoshop 1.0 is released.
  • 1990JASC Paint Shop Pro is first released.
  • 1990ARPANET is formally decommissioned, having fully evolved into the modern internet.
  • 1990Tim Berners-Lee creates the first browser, WorldWideWeb, at CERN.
  • 1991Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web, built at CERN two years earlier, is made publicly available.
  • 1991AOL begins offering dial-up access to the wider internet, rather than just its own proprietary network.
  • 1992Tripod is founded by Williams College classmates Bo Peabody and Brett Hershey with economics professor Dick Sabot, originally offering advice and tools for young adults rather than a web platform.
  • 1993NCSA Mosaic popularizes graphical web browsing.
  • 15 Dec 1994Netscape Navigator 1.0 is released, becoming the dominant browser of the early commercial web.
  • 1 Oct 1994The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is founded by Tim Berners-Lee.
  • 1994WorldWideWeb, renamed Nexus, is discontinued.
  • Nov 1994GeoCities is founded as Beverly Hills Internet — widely credited as the first major free personal-website hosting service (renamed GeoCities in 1995).
  • 1994Jim Bumgardner begins developing The Palace at Time Warner Interactive.
  • 1995As the Web expands, Tripod pivots to offering free, ad-supported homepage building and hosting.
  • 1995Newgrounds begins as Tom Fulp's personal website, eventually growing into a major hub for independent web animation, games, and Flash culture.
  • 1995Microsoft FrontPage makes visual website building accessible to non-programmers.
  • 16 Aug 1995Internet Explorer 1.0 is released, bundled with the Windows 95 Plus Pack.
  • 24 Aug 1995Windows 95 is released, bringing the internet and a PC within reach of the mainstream household for the first time.
  • Feb 1995Purikura ("Print Club") photo-sticker booths debut in Japan, developed by Atlus with Sega.
  • Nov 1995The Palace launches publicly.
  • Dec 1995Melicia Greenwood creates her first doll on The Palace, a goth "Barbie" sized so six of its nine avatar props hold interchangeable clothing — the starting point for "dollz," which soon diversify into skater, prep, and tiny styles before migrating off The Palace onto personal websites by the late 1990s.
  • 15 Dec 1995AltaVista launches, becoming the dominant search engine of the pre-Google web.
  • 1996Angelfire is founded, originally combining website building with an unrelated medical-transcription service.
  • 1996ezboard launches as a free forum-hosting service.
  • 1996Macromedia acquires FutureWave Software and renames FutureSplash Animator to Macromedia Flash, beginning Flash's major role in web animation and interactive media.
  • 10 May 1996The Internet Archive is founded by Brewster Kahle, beginning the crawl-and-preserve project that would later save much of the era this timeline covers.
  • 1996WebTV launches, a set-top box and online service that let people browse the web and send email on a television instead of a computer. A small circle of WebTV users passing animations to one another by email in early 2001 is the traceable origin of the glitter tile family preserved in this editor.
  • 15 Nov 1996ICQ launches, one of the first mass-market instant messengers.
  • Jan 1997Development and support for NCSA Mosaic ends.
  • 1997Microsoft buys WebTV Networks.
  • 1997Homestead is founded.
  • 1997FortuneCity launches as a free personal-web-hosting community, joining services such as GeoCities, Tripod, and Angelfire.
  • 1997Expage (Express Page) launches as a free personal-website hosting service.
  • 15 Sep 1997GeoCities Japan launches as a joint venture between the American GeoCities and SoftBank.
  • 1997WhoWhere acquires Angelfire.
  • 1 May 1997AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) is released, introducing buddy lists, custom screen names, and away messages that became a major outlet for online self-expression.
  • Jan 1998Netscape open-sources its browser code as the Mozilla project, the codebase that eventually becomes Firefox.
  • 9 Mar 1998Yahoo! Pager launches (renamed Yahoo! Messenger in 1999).
  • 1998Adobe ImageReady 1.0 is released.
  • Feb 1998Lycos acquires Tripod for $58 million in stock.
  • Aug 1998Lycos acquires WhoWhere for $133 million, bringing Angelfire under the same company as Tripod.
  • 4 Sep 1998Google is founded by Stanford PhD students Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
  • Sep 1998Google launches publicly with a "Cached" link built into its search results from the start, letting people view a page's last-crawled snapshot even when the live site was unavailable.
  • Oct 1998AOL Hometown launches, giving AOL subscribers free personal webpages.
  • 1998AOL acquires Netscape.
  • 4 Jan 1999Albino Blacksheep launches, becoming a major hub for viral Flash animation and animutation in the early 2000s.
  • 28 Jan 1999Yahoo! announces its acquisition of GeoCities (completed that May).
  • 18 Mar 1999LiveJournal launches, combining personal journals with social-networking features.
  • 1 Jun 1999Napster launches, founded by Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker, kicking off the peer-to-peer music-sharing era.
  • 22 Jul 1999MSN Messenger launches.
  • 23 Aug 1999Blogger launches, created by Pyra Labs, helping popularize easy web-based blogging.
  • 1999Xanga launches, initially focused on sharing book and music reviews before evolving into a major blogging and social-networking service.
  • 15 Nov 1999Neopets launches.
  • 1 Jan 2000ProBoards officially launches as a free forum-hosting service.
  • 1 Mar 2000Yahoo! Japan absorbs GeoCities Japan, renaming it Yahoo! GeoCities Japan.
  • 28 Mar 2000Yahoo! Photos launches as Yahoo!'s online photo-storage and sharing service.
  • 7 Aug 2000DeviantArt launches, developing into one of the web's largest communities for digital artists and fan-created artwork.
  • 2000LimeWire is founded by Mark Gorton.
  • 2001Freewebs launches as a free personal-website hosting service.
  • Early 2001A small circle of WebTV users trading animations by email, later remembered as the "Glitter Connection," produces the glitter tile family preserved in this editor. Mica's tile becomes the shared basis; Dan recolors it into flat jewel tones under his own gemstone names.
  • 30 Jan 2001Yahoo! Groups launches, combining mailing lists, forums, and file archives into one community platform (later peaking at over 100 million users).
  • Feb 2001Google acquires Deja.com's Usenet archive, Deja News (operational since March 1995), and relaunches it as Google Groups.
  • Feb 2001Habbo Hotel launches internationally, letting users decorate pixel-art rooms and avatars in a shared virtual space, following the earlier 2000 Finnish original.
  • 11 Jul 2001Napster shuts down its file-sharing service under a court injunction won by the RIAA.
  • 24 Oct 2001The Wayback Machine launches publicly, already containing over 10 billion archived pages.
  • 2001Communities.com folds in the dot-com collapse, ending official development of The Palace; the community keeps it running independently.
  • 2002Friendster is founded (it launches publicly the following year).
  • Sep 2002InvisionFree launches as a free remotely hosted forum service from Zathyus Networks.
  • 18 Feb 2003Gaia Online launches as Go-Gaia.com (renamed Gaia Online in 2004).
  • 2003Hi5 launches.
  • 2003ImageShack launches as a free image-hosting service widely used for externally hosted images on forums, blogs, and personal sites.
  • May 2003Photobucket launches, becoming one of the dominant image hosts for forums, blogs, profiles, and personal websites.
  • 15 Jul 2003The Mozilla Foundation is founded to carry the browser project forward as AOL scales back its involvement.
  • 1 Aug 2003MySpace launches.
  • 29 Aug 2003Skype is founded by Niklas Zennström (Sweden) and Janus Friis (Denmark), built by a team of Estonian engineers.
  • Sep 2003Delicious (del.icio.us) launches, popularizing social bookmarking and tagging.
  • 24 Jan 2004Orkut launches, becoming especially popular in Brazil and India.
  • 4 Feb 2004Facebook launches.
  • 9 Feb 2004Flickr launches as an online photo-sharing community.
  • Feb 2004Yahoo! Search switches to its own in-house search index, ending its longtime reliance on Google to power results.
  • 2004TinyPic launches as a free image and video host.
  • 14 Oct 2004Corel acquires JASC Software, makers of Paint Shop Pro and Animation Shop.
  • 9 Nov 2004Firefox 1.0 is released.
  • c. 2004–06Boomspeed is active as an early image/file host (exact founding and closure dates are lost to time).
  • Jan 2005Michael and Xochi Birch launch Bebo, which becomes especially popular in the UK and Ireland.
  • 14 Feb 2005YouTube is founded (the site launches publicly later that year), rapidly becoming a major user-uploaded video platform.
  • 20 Mar 2005Yahoo! acquires Flickr, bringing the photo-sharing service into its growing Web 2.0 portfolio.
  • 18 Apr 2005Adobe announces its acquisition of Macromedia for about $3.4 billion, bringing Flash under Adobe.
  • 18 Jul 2005News Corp acquires MySpace's parent company, Intermix Media, for about $580 million.
  • 7 Oct 2005Google Reader launches, becoming a major hub for following blogs and websites via RSS.
  • 2005Jim Conning launches Piczo, a teen-focused website builder and social network.
  • 2005FortuneCity is acquired by Dotster.
  • 2006Microsoft discontinues FrontPage.
  • June 2006Blingee launches as part of the Bauer Teen Network.
  • 15 Jul 2006Twitter launches publicly, becoming one of the defining social platforms of the Web 2.0 era.
  • 9 Oct 2006Google acquires YouTube for $1.65 billion (the deal closes that November).
  • 1 Feb 2007Polyvore launches, founded by three former Yahoo! engineers as a social-commerce site where users create fashion, beauty, and interior-design collages called "sets."
  • 19 Feb 2007Tumblr launches.
  • 2007We Heart It is founded by Fabio Giolito, initially as a visual-bookmarking tool before developing into an image-based social network centered on collecting and sharing inspirational imagery.
  • 1 Mar 2007Expage shuts down completely.
  • 2007ZetaBoards begins public testing as Zathyus Networks' next-generation forum platform, succeeding InvisionFree.
  • Mar 2007Adobe ImageReady is discontinued, folded into Photoshop CS3.
  • 20 Sep 2007Yahoo! Photos shuts down, with Yahoo! directing users to Flickr and other photo services.
  • 26 Nov 2007Intuit acquires Homestead.
  • 15 Jan 2008ezboard's homepage begins redirecting to its successor, Yuku, as communities are moved over rather than the service simply closing.
  • 2008AOL buys Bebo for $850 million.
  • 1 Mar 2008AOL ends development and support for Netscape's browsers.
  • 2 Sep 2008Google Chrome launches.
  • 31 Oct 2008AOL Hometown shuts down.
  • 14 Nov 2008Freewebs is renamed Webs.
  • 2009WhatsApp is founded.
  • May 2009MySpace is overtaken by Facebook in US unique visitors, ending its run as the largest social network.
  • 3 Jun 2009Bing launches, replacing Microsoft's earlier Live Search.
  • 2009Tripod stops offering new free webpages, becoming a paid-only service; existing free pages stay online.
  • 27 Oct 2009GeoCities (US) shuts down.
  • 2010Angelfire undergoes a major redesign and stops creating new classic free sites, though existing free pages stay online for years to come.
  • Mar 2010Pinterest launches, centered around image bookmarking, collections, and visual discovery.
  • 6 Oct 2010Instagram launches.
  • 26 Oct 2010LimeWire is ordered to shut down after a four-year RIAA lawsuit.
  • 2010M.I.A.'s "XXXO" references the Blingee aesthetic.
  • May 2011Yahoo! Search begins offering its own cached-page links, by way of the search technology it now shares with Microsoft's Bing.
  • 2011Friendster relaunches as a social-gaming site, dropping its original social-networking features.
  • 10 May 2011Microsoft announces its acquisition of Skype for $8.5 billion.
  • 29 Jun 2011Specific Media, with Justin Timberlake as co-owner, buys MySpace from News Corp for $35 million and relaunches it.
  • Sep 2011CrowdGather acquires Yuku and the legacy ezboard domains, after earlier ownership stints under KickApps and Inform Technologies.
  • Sep 2011Snapchat launches, relaunched from the earlier Picaboo app.
  • 28 Dec 2011Vistaprint acquires Webs for roughly $117.5 million.
  • 30 Apr 2012FortuneCity ends its free web-hosting service, citing rising costs that made it financially unsustainable, and directs users toward paid hosting — taking another GeoCities-era personal-hosting platform offline.
  • Nov 2012Piczo shuts down after two acquisitions.
  • 24 Jan 2013Vine launches, popularizing 6-second looping videos.
  • Feb 2013GIPHY is founded.
  • 15 Mar 2013Microsoft shuts down MSN/Windows Live Messenger worldwide outside China, pushing users to Skype.
  • 6 May 2013Adobe announces Creative Cloud will become its only option going forward, ending perpetual-license sales of Photoshop and the rest of Creative Suite.
  • 20 May 2013Yahoo! announces its acquisition of Tumblr for approximately $1.1 billion.
  • 28 Jun 2013Neocities launches.
  • 1 Jul 2013Google shuts down Google Reader.
  • 8 Jul 2013Yahoo! shuts down AltaVista.
  • 7 Aug 2013Bebo's founders buy it back from AOL for $1 million and shut it down immediately after.
  • 30 Sep 2013Microsoft shuts down WebTV, renamed MSN TV in July 2001, ending the service.
  • 19 Feb 2014Facebook announces its acquisition of WhatsApp for about $19 billion (the deal closes that October).
  • 2014Bebo relaunches as a messaging app, the first of several product pivots (through streaming and esports) over the next few years.
  • 2014Tenor is founded.
  • 2014Homestead is formally discontinued.
  • Sep 2014Google shuts down Orkut.
  • 2015Friendster shuts down for good.
  • 29 Jul 2015Microsoft Edge launches alongside Windows 10, positioned to replace Internet Explorer as Microsoft's default browser.
  • 31 Jul 2015Yahoo! announces its acquisition of Polyvore for a reported $200 million or more; Polyvore continues operating normally under Yahoo.
  • Aug 2015Blingee's near-shutdown is averted by user outcry and emergency funding.
  • 2016Tapatalk acquires Yuku.
  • Oct 2016The Internet Archive launches GifCities, for its own 20th anniversary.
  • 27 Oct 2016Twitter announces it's discontinuing Vine, disabling new uploads while leaving viewing and downloads active.
  • 17 Jan 2017Twitter officially shuts down Vine; the app's remaining functionality is discontinued a few months later.
  • 20 Jan 2017Twitter launches an online archive of every Vine video ever published.
  • 2017Tapatalk acquires Zathyus Networks, bringing InvisionFree and ZetaBoards under its umbrella.
  • 2017Tapatalk migrates Yuku's forums onto its own platform, ending Yuku as a standalone service.
  • 2017Verizon completes its acquisition of Yahoo!'s operating business, placing Tumblr and Polyvore under the new Oath subsidiary.
  • 2017Delicious effectively shuts down after several ownership changes.
  • 28 Jun 2017Photobucket disables free hotlinking, breaking embedded images across the web unless users pay.
  • 15 Dec 2017AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) shuts down after 20 years.
  • 2018InvisionFree and ZetaBoards are wound down as their communities are migrated to Tapatalk Groups.
  • 27 Mar 2018Google acquires Tenor.
  • 5 Apr 2018SSENSE acquires Polyvore from Oath and shuts it down immediately, redirecting the site to SSENSE — a notorious loss of user-created web content.
  • Apr 2018The Vine archive is officially discontinued.
  • 17 Jul 2018Yahoo! Messenger shuts down.
  • 31 Mar 2019GeoCities Japan shuts down, nearly a decade after its American counterpart.
  • 18 Mar 2019MySpace confirms a botched server migration permanently deleted 12 years of user content (2003–2015): over 50 million tracks from roughly 14 million artists, plus millions of personal photos and videos, early blog posts, comments, and private messages.
  • 18 Jun 2019Twitch acquires Bebo for up to $25 million to bolster its esports efforts.
  • 12 Aug 2019Automattic acquires Tumblr from Verizon.
  • 16 Sep 2019TinyPic shuts down, redirecting users to Photobucket.
  • May 2020Meta acquires GIPHY.
  • 15 Dec 2020Yahoo! Groups shuts down, deleting its archives.
  • 31 Dec 2020Adobe ends support for Flash Player.
  • 2021Klipy is founded.
  • 2021Austrian brothers Julian and Paul Zehetmayr acquire the LimeWire brand and its assets.
  • 2021We Heart It removes several social features, including articles, messages, and some community functionality, as the platform changes direction.
  • 29 Jan 2021A private-beta revival of Bebo is announced.
  • 7 Oct 2021VerticalScope acquires ProBoards' assets for $4.2 million; the service continues operating.
  • 28 Oct 2021Facebook rebrands its parent company as Meta.
  • May 2022The private-beta Bebo revival shuts down.
  • 14 Mar 2022Steve Wilhite, engineering lead on the GIF format, passes away.
  • 9 May 2022LimeWire relaunches, more than a decade after shutting down, as an NFT marketplace.
  • 15 Jun 2022Internet Explorer is officially retired, with Microsoft directing users to Edge.
  • 27 Oct 2022Elon Musk completes his acquisition of Twitter for $44 billion.
  • 23 May 2023Shutterstock acquires GIPHY from Meta, after UK regulators force a divestiture.
  • 23 Jul 2023Musk rebrands Twitter as X, retiring the bird logo.
  • 2023Webs shuts down.
  • 2023We Heart It effectively ends its original social-image platform, shifting toward a mobile photo-editing app model.
  • 2 Feb 2024Google retires its "Cached" page feature, citing improved page reliability across the modern web.
  • 22 Feb 2024Google Groups stops supporting posting or viewing new Usenet content; existing archives remain available.
  • 26 Jun 2024ICQ shuts down after nearly 28 years.
  • June 2024Blingee closes permanently.
  • Sep 2024Google and the Internet Archive announce a collaboration linking to the Wayback Machine directly from Google Search results.
  • 11 Dec 2024Bing retires its web-caching feature, following Google's lead.
  • late 2024Yahoo! Search's cache links quietly stop working as its Bing-powered backend loses the feature, with no official announcement.
  • 5 May 2025Microsoft retires Skype after 22 years, shifting users to Teams.
  • 30 Sep 2025AOL shuts down its dial-up internet service after 34 years.
  • 2026A new Piczo pre-launch site appears, teasing a possible revival.
  • Jan 2026A major outage leaves Angelfire's user-hosted sites inaccessible.
  • 6 Mar 2026Lycos announces the final closure of both Angelfire and Tripod.
  • 24 Apr 2026Angelfire and Tripod shut down for good under Lycos.
  • 30 Jun 2026Google deprecates Tenor's public API.
  • 2026Bebo returns again.
  • 1 Sep 2026Bebo closes.
